name: Guildford Cathedral
text: Your train passes near Guildford Cathedral, on the train's {side}, on top of Stag Hill. Designed by Edward Maufe and built between 1936 and 1961, it was the last Church of England cathedral to be consecrated on a new site.

name: St Catherine's Chapel, Guildford
text: Your train passes near the ruined chapel on St Catherine's Hill, on the train's {side}, built early in the 14th century; the railway runs through a tunnel under the hill. J. M. W. Turner drew the hill and chapel, and in 2020 work on the line uncovered a small sandstone cave with carved niches, thought to be a medieval shrine.

name: Charterhouse School
text: Your train passes near Charterhouse, on the train's {side}, a school founded by Thomas Sutton in 1611 on the site of a Carthusian monastery in London. It moved here in 1872, to a hilltop site just outside Godalming.

name: The Pepperpot, Godalming
text: Your train passes near the Pepperpot in Godalming High Street, on the train's {side}, a little market hall with a clock tower and cupola, finished in 1814. Markets were held under its arches, and the room upstairs housed the town's museum from 1921 to 1987.

name: Tigbourne Court
text: Your train passes near Tigbourne Court, on the train's {side}, a country house by Edwin Lutyens, finished in 1901 and called "probably his best" building. Edgar Horne, who had it built, never moved in, and it was let to the fraudster Whitaker Wright.

name: Haslemere Educational Museum
text: Your train passes near Haslemere Educational Museum, on the train's {side}, founded in 1888 by the surgeon Sir Jonathan Hutchinson for his natural history collection. It holds nearly half a million specimens, artefacts, papers and images, among them the mummy of Pa-Er-Abu, thought to have been an Egyptian priest.

name: Haslemere
text: Your train passes near Haslemere, on the train's {side}, thought to have begun as a planned town in the 12th century, with a market charter from 1221. The Dolmetsch Early Music Festival was founded here in 1925, and at the west end of Shottermill, in the same parish, Surrey, Hampshire and West Sussex meet.

name: Liss Riverside Railway Walk North
text: Your train passes near Liss Riverside Railway Walk, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve whose footpath runs through willow and alder woodland along the route of the Longmoor Military Railway, from Liss to Liss Forest.

name: Statue of William III, Petersfield
text: Your train passes near the statue of William III in Petersfield's square, on the train's {side}, a lead figure of the king as a Roman senator on horseback, made in about 1757 and once gilded. It first stood at the entrance to Petersfield House and was moved to the square when the house was pulled down in the 1790s.

name: St Hubert's Church, Idsworth
text: Your train passes near St Hubert's Church at Idsworth, on the train's {side}, the only place of worship of an isolated hamlet in the South Downs, with medieval paintings on its north wall and around the east window. The diocese calls it "the little church in the field".

name: Rowland's Castle
text: Your train passes the remains of Rowland's Castle, on the train's {side}, a motte-and-bailey castle built at some time between 1066 and 1189, where Henry II spent several days hunting. The railway and quarrying damaged the site in the 19th century, and only earthworks and a few bits of wall are left.

name: Havant
text: Your train passes near the middle of Havant, on the train's {side}, once home to the leading parchment works in southern England, which closed in 1936. The Treaty of Versailles was written on Havant parchment.

name: The Elms, Bedhampton
text: Your train passes near The Elms in Old Bedhampton, on the train's {side}, a 17th-century house given a Gothic Revival makeover in the 18th. Its owner, Sir Theophilus Lee, invited his relative the Duke of Wellington to dine here, and had a room made in his honour.

name: Portsmouth Airport
text: Your train passes the site of Portsmouth Airport, on the train's {side}, opened in 1932 with three grass runways between Hilsea and Langstone Harbour. From here ran the first air ferry in the south of England, to Ryde on the Isle of Wight; the last flight left on December 31st 1973.

name: Warblington Castle
text: Your train passes near Warblington Castle, on the train's {side}, a moated manor built between 1515 and 1525 for Margaret Pole, Countess of Salisbury. Most of it was destroyed in the Civil War, and only a gate tower, part of a wall and a gateway still stand.

name: Emsworth
text: Your train passes near Emsworth, on the train's {side}, at the head of an arm of Chichester Harbour, with a basin that fills at high tide and can be emptied through a sluice. The River Ems is named after the town, not the other way round: the chronicler Raphael Holinshed gave it the name in the 16th century.

name: Brook Meadow
text: Your train passes near Brook Meadow, on the train's {side}, a nature reserve of grassland and woodland between two streams on the edge of Emsworth, looked after by volunteers. Its wildlife includes water voles.

name: Southbourne
text: Your train passes near Southbourne, on the train's {side}, a village that began in 1876, when its church of St John was consecrated. It sits in the western corner of West Sussex, with the Hampshire border just to the west.

name: Nutbourne
text: Your train passes near Nutbourne, on the train's {side}, a village at the northern tip of Thorney Channel, an inlet of Chichester Harbour. Its name probably comes from the South Saxons' hnutu burna, the stream overhung by nut trees.

name: Fishbourne Roman Palace
text: Your train passes near Fishbourne Roman Palace, on the train's {side}, the largest known Roman home north of the Alps, built around AD 75. Its mosaics include the Dolphin mosaic, and it burnt down in about 270, after which it was abandoned.

name: Chichester Cathedral
text: Your train passes near Chichester Cathedral, on the train's {side}, founded in 1075. It is the only medieval cathedral in England with a bell tower standing apart from the church, and its spire is the only one of a medieval English cathedral that can be seen from the sea.

name: Chichester Cross
text: Your train passes near Chichester Cross, on the train's {side}, an elaborate stone market cross about 50 feet tall, where the city's four main streets meet. Its inscription says Bishop Edward Story built it, so that poor people would have somewhere to sell their wares.

name: Bognor Regis
text: Your train passes near Bognor Regis, on the train's {side}, a resort laid out by Sir Richard Hotham in the late 18th century on an empty stretch of coast. King George V spent three months recovering here in 1929, and the town was given the name "Regis" later that year.

name: John Baker's Mill, Barnham
text: Your train passes near John Baker's Mill at Barnham, on the train's {side}, a flint and stone tower windmill built in 1829. It was worked by wind until the early 1920s and by engine until 1963.

name: St Mary Magdalene's Church, Tortington
text: Your train passes near St Mary Magdalene's Church at Tortington, on the train's {side}, founded in the 12th century and little changed since. Its chancel arch and doorway are carved with rare beakhead figures, described as "grotesque, boggle-eyed monsters".

name: Slayer's Slab, Lyminster
text: Your train passes near Lyminster church, on the train's {side}, home of the Slayer's Slab, a medieval gravestone with a cross on it and no name. Legend says it marks the grave of the man who killed the Knucker, the dragon of the nearby knuckerhole.

name: St Nicholas Church, Poling
text: Your train passes near St Nicholas Church at Poling, on the train's {side}, a flint church whose nave dates from Saxon times. A Saxon window found in its north wall in 1917 still has part of its original wooden shutter.

name: St Mary's Church, Goring-by-Sea
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church at Goring-by-Sea, on the train's {side}, a Norman church given its present Gothic Revival look by Decimus Burton in 1837. Inside is a mural painted in 1954 by the German artist Hans Feibusch, which caused controversy at the time.

name: English Martyrs' Church, Goring-by-Sea
text: Your train passes near English Martyrs' Church in Goring-by-Sea, on the train's {side}, whose ceiling is a copy of Michelangelo's Sistine Chapel ceiling, painted by hand by the sign-painter Gary Bevans between 1987 and 1993. The church is the same width as the Sistine Chapel, and a little shorter.

name: West Tarring
text: Your train passes near West Tarring, on the train's {side}, a village given to the archbishops of Canterbury in the 10th century, with a 13th-century Archbishop's Palace. Tradition says Thomas Becket visited, and it had a much-visited fig garden from 1745 or earlier.

name: Teville Stream
text: Your train passes near the Teville Stream, on the train's {side}, which rises at allotments in Tarring and runs through Worthing to the sea. It was once tidal and much wider; now it runs in culverts for much of its length.

name: Beach House, Worthing
text: Your train passes near Beach House in Worthing, on the train's {side}, a Regency villa built in 1820. King Edward VII stayed here several times between 1907 and 1910, and in 1936 it took in children from the Basque country, fleeing the Spanish Civil War.

name: Lancing Carriage Works
text: Your train passes the site of Lancing Carriage Works, on the train's {side}, where railway carriages and wagons were built and repaired from 1911 to 1965. A special daily train, known as the Lancing Belle, brought the workers from Brighton.

name: Brighton City Airport
text: Your train passes near Shoreham Airport, on the train's {side}, the oldest airport in the UK. The first flight from here was in 1910, it opened officially in 1911, and its terminal is a listed 1930s Art Deco building.

name: Shoreham Redoubt
text: Your train passes near Shoreham Fort, on the train's {side}, built at the mouth of the River Adur and finished in June 1857, at a time of political alarm. Its gun platform is shaped like a straight-sided crescent, ringed by a ditch with a loopholed wall along the middle.

name: St Michael and All Angels Church, Southwick
text: Your train passes near St Michael and All Angels Church in Southwick, on the train's {side}, rebuilt in the 12th and 13th centuries with some Anglo-Saxon work still in place. A church may have stood here as early as the 10th century.

name: Portslade Town Hall
text: Your train passes near Portslade Town Hall, on the train's {side}, built in 1928 as the Ronuk Hall, a social club for the workers of a local polish factory. It later became the meeting place of the town's council.

name: British Engineerium
text: Your train passes near the Goldstone Pumping Station in Hove, on the train's {side}, a set of High Victorian Gothic buildings begun in 1866. It pumped water for Hove and Brighton for more than a century, and later became the British Engineerium, a museum of engineering and steam power.

name: Goldstone Ground
text: Your train passes the site of the Goldstone Ground, on the train's {side}, home of Brighton & Hove Albion from 1902 to 1997. It hosted football at the 1948 Olympic Games, and David Beckham made his professional debut here in 1992.

name: Preston Manor
text: Your train passes near Preston Manor, on the train's {side}, a manor house rebuilt in 1738 around part of a 13th-century building. It has been a museum of Edwardian life since 1932, and is said to be one of the most haunted buildings in Britain.
